## Data Suppression {.pause}

-   Surveys (based on probability samples) often have large sample sizes
    (relative to other study designs)

-   However, some point estimates may still be quite variable
    (imprecise/large variance)

    -   For example, for a subpopulation that is small and was not
        purposely oversampled

-   Additionally, some estimates based on small numbers of people, or
    estimates for population groups that are small, might be **dangerous
    in terms of privacy**

> [**Suppression**]{.alert} = Purposefully withholding / not releasing a
> specific estimate (to the public)

. . .

-   Different statistical agencies use different rules about when to
    *suppress* results

    -   Possible Reason 1: limit risk of disclosure -- i.e., that you
        could figure out who answered the survey

    -   Possible Reason 2: estimate is deemed "too variable" or "too
        unreliable"

## Data Suppression Rules: Examples {.pause}

-   [**Population Thresholds**]{.alert}

    -   Only release estimates for areas/population groups that exceed a
        certain size

        -   Example: *Areas or groups of 65,000 or more are eligible for
            estimates to be released*\
            (American Community Survey, ACS)

<p>

. . .

-   [**Restrictions on Numerators and/or Denominators of
    Proportions**]{.alert}

    -   Based on the **unweighted** sample, suppress estimates with too
        few cases in the numerator or denominator of a proportion

        -   Example: *Suppress estimates based on proportions with
            numerator \<10*\
            (National Crime Victimization Survey, NCVS)

        -   Example: *Suppress estimates based on proportions with
            denominator \<30*\
            (National Survey of Family Growth, NSFG)

## Data Suppression Rules: Examples (con't)

-   [**Relative Standard Error (RSE)**]{.alert} = SE of estimate, divided by estimate, times 100

    -   $\displaystyle{RSE = 100 \times \frac{\widehat{SE}(\bar{y})}{|\bar{y}|}}$

    -   Usually a cutoff (threshold) is chosen and estimates with **RSE above the
    threshold are suppressed**

        -   Example: *Suppress estimates with RSE \>30%*\
        (National Health Interview Survey, NHIS)
        
        -   Example: *BRFSS results in the [MMWR Table](#slide-table): Suppress estimates with RSE \> 30%*

    -   Sometimes RSE is modified for proportions:
    $$\frac{\widehat{SE}(\hat{p})/\hat{p}}{-\mathrm{ln}(\hat{p})}>.175$$
    when $\hat{p} \le$ 0.5

## RSE: Why Modify for p < 0.5?

A visualization of RSE (for an SRS) as a function of p is helpful:

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "A plot showing two curves, RSE and RSE divided by the negative natural log of the proportion, against a Proportion value from 0 to 1. The RSE curve spikes steeply near 0, whereas the RSE/-ln(p) does not have as steep an increase near 0."
library(tidyverse)
dat <- tibble(n = 1000, 
              p = seq(0.001,1,.001),
              se_p = sqrt(p*(1-p)/n),
              rse_orig = 100*se_p / p,
              rse_alt = case_when(p <= 0.5 ~ rse_orig/(-log(p)),
                                  .default = NA)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(rse_orig,rse_alt), 
               values_to = "rse", names_to = "estimator") %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(est = case_when(estimator == "rse_orig" ~ "RSE",
                         estimator == "rse_alt" ~ "RSE/-ln(p)"))
theme_set(theme_bw())
dat %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = rse, group = est, color = est)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = filter(dat, p == 0.001),
                           aes(label = est), size = 5) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 14)) +
  labs(x = "Proportion", y = "RSE") + 
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2")
```

(n is set to 1,000 for the purposes of this visualization)

## Combining Survey Waves {.pause}

-   Many surveys are repeated (e.g., yearly, every 2 years) to monitor
    trends

-   Combining **across survey waves** can also be used to estimate
    characteristics from small subpopulations

-   Generally speaking, these are two different possible goals of
    combining survey waves:

. . .

1.  Estimate a *change* in a mean/proportion and test the significance
    of the change

    -   Example: Has the proportion of children aged 3-17 diagnosed with
        anxiety changed from 2017 to 2020? What is the estimate of the
        change?

. . .

2.  Estimate a mean/proportion using data from multiple years *assuming
    that the mean/proportion has not changed over time*

    -   Example: What is the (average) proportion of children aged 3-17
        with an Autism Spectrum Disorder in the years 2017-2020?

. . .

-   Assuming that **a new (cross-sectional) sample is taken each wave**
    (i.e., not a panel/longitudinal survey), samples from wave to wave
    are **independent**

-   Thus combining across waves is straightfoward (it is what was done
    to produce [the BFRSS table](#slide-table))

## Estimating Changes {.pause}

-   As long as the samples each year/wave are drawn independently:

| Year | True Population Value | Estimate | Variance of Estimate |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| 1 | $\theta_1$ | $\hat{\theta}_1$ | $V(\hat{\theta}_1)$ |
| 2 | $\theta_2$ | $\hat{\theta}_2$ | $V(\hat{\theta}_2)$ |
| Change | $\Delta = \theta_2-\theta_1$ | $\hat{\Delta}=\hat{\theta}_2-\hat{\theta}_1$ | $V(\hat{\Delta}) = V(\hat{\theta}_1) + V(\hat{\theta}_2)$ |

-   Since $\hat{\theta}_1$ and $\hat{\theta}_2$ are **independent**, there is no covariance term!

-   Calculate estimates in each year/wave, subtract to estimate the
    change, add the (estimated) variances to obtain the variance of the
    change, and test for change...

. . .

...or you can **pool the data from the waves** and let software do the
analysis for you!

-   Benefit to using software: can conduct more sophisticated analyses
    (e.g., test for linear change trend, adjust for covariates, etc.)

## Combining Waves of the Same Survey {.pause}

-   Two things to be careful about when pooling survey years:

1.  Is the design the same in each year? E.g., strata, clustering, etc.

    -   For many large surveys the answer will be yes -- precisely
        because they want to facilitate trend analyses

    -   If differences in strata definitions, may have to redefine to
        align correctly (e.g., "stratum 1", "stratum 2" for all waves)

. . .

2.  The sample weights -- rescale or not rescaled?

    -   Estimating changes in means/proportions -- does not matter
        whether you rescale weights or not, estimates identical

    -   Pooled estimates (e.g., prevalence in 2017-2020) --
        rescale weights so sum is the average population size by
        dividing by number of waves being combined

        -   Technically, prevalence estimates will be identical
            with/without rescaling -- but population counts will only be
            correct if you rescale
